steps.title: Validate the species and conditions
steps.summary: All 4 species can be read, the roles make an experiment and the conditions are physical.
details: Species: NO(g): reactant, nitric oxide; O3(g): reactant, ozone; NO2(g): product, nitrogen dioxide; O2(g): product, oxygen.
Conditions: 298 K, 1 bar, 300 s, environment gas-phase.

steps.title: Check conservation of atoms and charge
steps.summary: Balanced with the proportions of a sourced elementary reaction, because conservation alone leaves them open: NO(g) + O3(g) -> NO2(g) + O2(g).
details: Conservation of the elements and the charge leaves 2 independent solutions for these species, so it does not fix the proportions. The proportions used are those of the reaction "Nitric oxide + ozone" as it is printed on data sheet I.A3.54 of the IUPAC evaluation, which lists it as an elementary reaction: NO(g) + O3(g) -> NO2(g) + O2(g).
Atoms on the reactant side and on the product side: N 1 = 1, O 4 = 4.
Charge on the reactant side and on the product side: 0 = 0.
Balancing is bookkeeping: it shows that the equation is possible, not that the reaction takes place.

steps.title: Select the models that apply
steps.summary: Thermodynamics and kinetics are both selected.
details: Stoichiometry: applies. The equation is balanced.
Thermodynamics: selected. Standard reaction enthalpy, entropy, Gibbs energy and equilibrium constant from the reference table, as far as the table covers the species.
Kinetics: selected. Nitric oxide + ozone: rate = k [NO] [O3]; d[NO]/dt = -rate, d[O3]/dt = -rate, d[NO2]/dt = +rate, d[O2]/dt = +rate. The expression is recommended for 195 K to 308 K.

steps.title: Look up the reference data
steps.summary: Every species of the equation is in the reference table. The rate expression comes from a cited data sheet.
details: NO(g): nitrogen monoxide (nitric oxide) (NIST Chemistry WebBook, NIST Standard Reference Database Number 69); ΔfH° = 90.29 kJ/mol; S° = 210.76 J/(mol K), as printed by the source.
O3(g): ozone (NIST Chemistry WebBook, NIST Standard Reference Database Number 69); ΔfH° = 142.67 kJ/mol; S° = 238.92 J/(mol K), as printed by the source.
NO2(g): nitrogen dioxide (NIST Chemistry WebBook, NIST Standard Reference Database Number 69); ΔfH° = 33.10 kJ/mol; S° = 240.04 J/(mol K), as printed by the source.
O2(g): oxygen (CODATA Key Values for Thermodynamics); ΔfH° = 0 kJ/mol (zero by definition); S° = 205.152 ± 0.005 J/(mol K), as printed by the source.
Rate expression: Nitric oxide + ozone, data sheet I.A3.54 of the IUPAC evaluation (journal pages 1574-1575): k = 1.4 × 10⁻¹² cm³ molecule⁻¹ s⁻¹ × exp(−1310 K / T), recommended for 195 K to 308 K.

The same expression as extracted from the PDF of the source, where superscripts and minus signs appear as plain characters: "k = 1.4×10−12 exp(−1310/T ) cm3 molecule−1 s−1 over the temperature range 195–308 K."
Reliability stated by the evaluators: Δlog10 k = ±0.08 at 298 K and Δ(E/R) = ±200 K, expanded uncertainties of about 95 % confidence.

steps.title: Name the calculation engine
steps.summary: Engines used: exact rational balancing, Hess's law on reference values and Dormand-Prince 5(4) integration of the rate law.
details: Balancing: exact rational null space of the element-and-charge composition matrix, scaled to the smallest whole numbers; no floating-point arithmetic.

Thermodynamics: Hess's law on the tabulated standard enthalpies of formation and standard entropies at 298.15 K; ΔG°(T) = ΔH°(298.15 K) − T·ΔS°(298.15 K) with the reaction enthalpy and entropy taken as independent of temperature; K = exp(−ΔG°/RT); uncertainties of the table values combined in quadrature.

Kinetics: rate constant k = A·exp(−Ea/RT) from the data sheet; concentrations by Dormand-Prince 5(4) explicit Runge-Kutta with adaptive step size and fourth-order dense output, error tolerance 1e-8, at most 200000 step attempts, 201 output points.
Engine: @matterlab/reactions 0.1.0. It is deterministic: no clock and no random numbers are used.

steps.title: Run the calculation
steps.summary: Calculated: thermodynamic values from the reference table and the rate constant and the concentration curves.
details: Reaction enthalpy ΔrH°(298.15 K) = −199.86 kJ/mol; reaction entropy ΔrS°(298.15 K) = −4.49 J/(mol K).
Gibbs energy ΔrG°(298 K) = −198.52 kJ/mol; log10 K = 34.80, K ≈ 6.3 × 10³⁴.
With every species in its standard state the reaction is product-favoured.
Thermodynamics: closed-form sums over table values; there is nothing to converge.
Rate constant at 298 K: k = 1.7 × 10⁻¹⁴ cm³ molecule⁻¹ s⁻¹, uncertain by a factor of 1.2 according to the evaluators (about 95 % confidence).
The integration reached t = 300 s in 32 accepted steps (0 rejected, 194 evaluations of the rate law) at an error tolerance of 1e-8; the budget of 200000 step attempts was not exhausted.
Half-life of NO, the limiting reactant: 47 s (numerical quadrature of the rate law).

From t = 0 to t = 300 s: NO: 5.0 × 10¹¹ → 2.0 × 10¹⁰ molecule cm⁻³; O3: 1.0 × 10¹² → 5.2 × 10¹¹ molecule cm⁻³; NO2: 0 → 4.8 × 10¹¹ molecule cm⁻³; O2: 0 → 4.8 × 10¹¹ molecule cm⁻³; 96 % of NO has reacted.

steps.title: State the limitations
details: MATTER LAB did not predict this reaction: it evaluated the equation built from the species that were entered. A balanced equation is bookkeeping, not evidence that the reaction takes place.

Thermodynamic values refer to every species in its standard state (pure solids and liquids, ideal gases at 1 bar, ideal solutes). They are not the values of an actual mixture, and no equilibrium composition is computed.
A favourable Gibbs energy says nothing about rate: thermodynamics tells where the equilibrium lies, not how fast it is reached or whether the reaction starts at all without ignition or a catalyst.

The simulation follows one elementary step in isolation, at constant temperature in a perfectly mixed volume. It is not a model of a real mixture: further reactions of the products, competing reactions of the reactants and the reverse reaction are not included.
The rate expression is a gas-phase one, recommended by its source for 195 K to 308 K.

assumptions: All species are in their standard states: pure solids and liquids, ideal gases at 1 bar, and aqueous species in the solute standard state of the source table.

Reaction enthalpy and entropy follow from Hess's law: the sum over products minus the sum over reactants of the tabulated enthalpies of formation and standard entropies at 298.15 K, each multiplied by its coefficient.

The Gibbs energy at 298 K is estimated as ΔG°(T) ≈ ΔH°(298.15 K) − T ΔS°(298.15 K): the reaction enthalpy and entropy are taken as independent of temperature, which amounts to neglecting the difference in heat capacity between products and reactants, and no phase change between 298.15 K and T is considered.
K = exp(−ΔG°/RT) is the dimensionless thermodynamic equilibrium constant, expressed in activities relative to the standard states above.

The direction label compares ΔG° with RT and with its own uncertainty; it describes all species in their standard states, not an arbitrary mixture, and says nothing about how fast the reaction is or whether it proceeds at all.

beginner.heading: What this experiment asks
paragraphs: This experiment looks at the reaction **NO(g) + O3(g) -> NO2(g) + O2(g)**.
It asks how much heat the reaction gives out or takes in, which side of the reaction is favoured and how fast the starting substances are used up.
MATTER LAB works on the reaction you entered. It does not decide whether these substances really react.

beginner.heading: What goes in
paragraphs: Starting substances: nitric oxide (NO, gas) and ozone (O3, gas). Products entered: nitrogen dioxide (NO2, gas) and oxygen (O2, gas).
Temperature 298 K (25 °C), pressure 1 bar.
Starting amounts: NO(g) 5 × 10¹¹ molecule cm⁻³ and O3(g) 1 × 10¹² molecule cm⁻³, followed for 300 s.

beginner.heading: How it was worked out
paragraphs: First the equation was balanced, so that no atoms and no electric charge appear or disappear.
For these substances that rule alone leaves the proportions open, so the proportions of the published reaction between exactly these substances were used.
Then published reference values for each substance were added up, products minus starting substances. This is known as Hess's law. Nothing was simulated for it.
For the speed, a published rate constant for exactly this reaction was used, and the amounts were followed forward in time in many small steps.

beginner.heading: The idea behind the numbers: energy
paragraphs: The heat of reaction, written ΔH, is the heat content of the products minus that of the starting substances. A negative value means that heat is given out.
Whether a reaction is favoured depends on that heat and on the change in disorder (the entropy, ΔS). The two are combined in the Gibbs energy ΔG. A negative ΔG means that the products are favoured.

beginner.heading: The idea behind the numbers: speed
paragraphs: The rate of the reaction is proportional to how much of each reacting substance is present; square brackets stand for the amount in a given volume.
The rate constant k says how fast this particular reaction is at this temperature.

beginner.heading: What is assumed
paragraphs: Every substance is treated as pure and under standard conditions (a pressure of 1 bar).
Only this one reaction takes place, the mixture is perfectly stirred, and its temperature stays the same.

beginner.heading: What came out
paragraphs: Balanced equation: **NO(g) + O3(g) -> NO2(g) + O2(g)**.
Heat of reaction: **−199.86 kJ/mol** for the amounts in the equation, counted in moles. The minus sign means that heat is **given out** (the reaction is exothermic).
Gibbs energy at 298 K: **−198.52 kJ/mol**. The products are favoured.
Equilibrium constant: K ≈ 6.3 × 10³⁴. The larger this number, the further the balance lies towards the products.
Rate constant at 298 K: **k = 1.7 × 10⁻¹⁴ cm³ molecule⁻¹ s⁻¹**.
Half of the NO is used up after about **47 s**.
After 300 s, 96 % of it has reacted.

beginner.heading: How sure is this
paragraphs: The balanced equation is exact arithmetic; its numbers are certain.
The reference table gives no uncertainty for some of the values used, so none can be given for the result.
The published rate constant is itself uncertain by about a factor of 1.2.
These numbers carry the label "Computed": Produced by a real calculation. The method, settings and limitations are recorded.
Numbers are rounded so that they show no more digits than the data behind them support.

beginner.heading: Did the calculation finish
paragraphs: The step-by-step calculation ran to the end (32 steps) and met its accuracy target.

beginner.heading: What is not included
paragraphs: MATTER LAB did not predict that these substances react. It only did the sums for the reaction you entered.
The energy values are for pure substances under standard conditions, not for a real mixture.
Being favoured is not the same as being fast. A favoured reaction can be far too slow to notice, or may need a spark to start.
The simulation follows only this one reaction. In a real mixture other reactions happen at the same time.
The published speed data are for gases between 195 K and 308 K.

beginner.heading: Why reality may differ
paragraphs: Real mixtures are not under standard conditions: the actual pressures and concentrations shift the balance.
A favoured reaction can still be so slow that nothing visible happens, or it may need a spark or a catalyst to start.
In a real mixture other reactions use up or re-form the same substances, so the amounts change differently.
Real mixtures are not perfectly stirred and may warm up or cool down as they react.
The reaction that really happens may not be the one written down: other products can form.

advanced.heading: Objective
paragraphs: Evaluate the reaction NO(g) + O3(g) -> NO2(g) + O2(g) at 298 K and 1 bar: the balanced equation, the standard reaction enthalpy, entropy, Gibbs energy and equilibrium constant from reference data and the rate constant and concentration-time curves, if a sourced rate law exists for exactly this reaction.
Method requested: auto. The equation was built from the species entered as reactants and products; no product was predicted.

paragraphs: All species are in their standard states: pure solids and liquids, ideal gases at 1 bar, and aqueous species in the solute standard state of the source table.

The mixture is homogeneous, at constant temperature and constant volume.

advanced.heading: Results
paragraphs: Balanced equation: NO(g) + O3(g) -> NO2(g) + O2(g).
ΔrH°(298.15 K) = −199.86 kJ/mol, per mole of reaction as written.
Direction with every species in its standard state: product-favoured.
k(298 K) = 1.7 × 10⁻¹⁴ cm³ molecule⁻¹ s⁻¹.
Half-life of NO (limiting reactant): 47 s, by numerical quadrature of the rate law.
Concentrations from t = 0 to t = 300 s: NO: 5.0 × 10¹¹ → 2.0 × 10¹⁰ molecule cm⁻³; O3: 1.0 × 10¹² → 5.2 × 10¹¹ molecule cm⁻³; NO2: 0 → 4.8 × 10¹¹ molecule cm⁻³; O2: 0 → 4.8 × 10¹¹ molecule cm⁻³.

Energy diagram: Ea = 10.9 ± 1.7 kJ/mol (E/R = 1310 K ± 200 K), from the temperature dependence of the evaluated rate expression (data sheet I.A3.54 of the IUPAC evaluation). It is an empirical Arrhenius activation energy, not a computed transition state: no transition-state structure or energy was calculated, and it differs from an enthalpy of activation by a term of the order of RT (2.5 kJ/mol at 298 K).

advanced.heading: Confidence and uncertainty
paragraphs: Stoichiometric coefficients are exact (rational arithmetic).

No uncertainty is given for the reaction enthalpy because the source prints none for NO(g), O3(g), NO2(g). No uncertainty is given for the reaction entropy because the source prints none for NO(g), O3(g), NO2(g).
Evidence: reaction enthalpy and entropy are computed from reference data; the Gibbs energy and equilibrium constant are labelled computed.

Values from 2 reference tables are combined (CODATA Key Values for Thermodynamics; NIST Chemistry WebBook, NIST Standard Reference Database Number 69). They were evaluated separately and are not guaranteed to be mutually consistent.

Reliability of the rate constant, from the evaluators' figures: Δlog10 k(T) = Δlog10 k(298 K) + 0.4343·Δ(E/R)·|1/T − 1/298| = 0.080, that is a factor of 1.2; an expanded uncertainty of about 95 % confidence, assigned by the evaluators.

The numerical error of the integration is controlled by the tolerance (1e-8, relative to the largest change each concentration can undergo); it is far smaller than the uncertainty of the rate constant. Evidence label of the kinetic results: computed.
The reaction enthalpy has no uncertainty and is rounded to 2 decimals, the fewest printed by the source among the enthalpies of formation used.
The Gibbs energy has no uncertainty and is rounded to 2 decimals, as far as the printed digits of the enthalpies and entropies used reach.
The equilibrium constant is given with at most two significant figures: the source states no uncertainty, so the printed digits of the Gibbs energy are the only guide to its precision.
Rate constants, half-lives and concentrations are given to two significant figures, the precision with which the source prints its rate parameters.

advanced.heading: Convergence status
paragraphs: Balancing: exact, nothing to converge.
Thermodynamics: closed-form sums over table values, nothing to converge.

Integrator: Dormand-Prince 5(4) explicit Runge-Kutta with adaptive step size and fourth-order dense output. Status: ok. Accepted steps: 32; rejected: 0; evaluations of the rate law: 194; tolerance: 1e-8; budget of 200000 step attempts not exhausted.

advanced.heading: Known limitations
paragraphs: MATTER LAB did not predict this reaction: it evaluated the equation built from the species that were entered. A balanced equation is bookkeeping, not evidence that the reaction takes place.

Thermodynamic values refer to every species in its standard state (pure solids and liquids, ideal gases at 1 bar, ideal solutes). They are not the values of an actual mixture, and no equilibrium composition is computed.
A favourable Gibbs energy says nothing about rate: thermodynamics tells where the equilibrium lies, not how fast it is reached or whether the reaction starts at all without ignition or a catalyst.

The simulation follows one elementary step in isolation, at constant temperature in a perfectly mixed volume. It is not a model of a real mixture: further reactions of the products, competing reactions of the reactants and the reverse reaction are not included.
The rate expression is a gas-phase one, recommended by its source for 195 K to 308 K.

advanced.heading: Why the prediction may not match reality
paragraphs: The equation as written may not be the reaction that occurs: side reactions, incomplete conversion and other products are not considered.
Composition and non-ideality: the driving force in an actual mixture is ΔG = ΔG° + RT ln Q with activities that differ from the standard states; neither Q nor activity coefficients are computed.
Kinetic hindrance: thermodynamics implies nothing about rate, and metastable mixtures are common.
Temperature dependence: heat capacities and any phase transition between 298.15 K and the temperature of the experiment are neglected.
Reference data: tabulated values carry their own uncertainties and, where two tables are combined, need not be mutually consistent.
Coupled chemistry: in any real mixture the reactants and products take part in other reactions, including the reverse one.
Rate data: the rate constant is an evaluated measurement with a stated reliability, recommended for a limited temperature range; pressure effects are not modelled beyond what the data sheet states.
Transport and heat: mixing, diffusion, wall reactions, photochemistry and the temperature change caused by the heat of reaction are neglected.
